lessons.title: Same Size or Not
lessons.concept: Equal Parts as the Condition for a Fraction

play.targetObjective: Decide whether a whole has been cut into equal parts.
stepByStep: Look along the parts, not at how many there are.
Compare two of them at a time.
If any two are different sizes, it is not a fair split.
A fraction only means something when every part is the same.
play.kidTip: Four pieces is not quarters unless all four are the same size.
play.audioPrompt: Are all the parts the same size?

prompts.default: Are all the parts the same size?

lessons.title: One of Them
lessons.concept: Naming One of a Number of Equal Parts

play.targetObjective: Name one part of a whole cut into equal parts.
stepByStep: Count how many equal parts the whole is cut into.
That number goes underneath.
One part is shaded, so a one goes on top.
One of four equal parts is one quarter.
play.kidTip: The number underneath tells you how many pieces the whole was cut into — not how big they are.
play.audioPrompt: One part is shaded. What is it called?

lessons.title: Half of What?
lessons.concept: A Fraction as a Quantity Only Once the Whole Is Named

play.targetObjective: Recognise that the same fraction of different wholes is different amounts.
stepByStep: Check the fraction shaded on each one. They are the same.
Now look at how big the two wholes are.
The same fraction of a bigger whole is a bigger amount.
A fraction on its own is not an amount until you say what it is a fraction of.
play.kidTip: Half a biscuit and half a cake are both a half. They are not both the same amount of food.
play.audioPrompt: Both have the same fraction shaded. Which is more?

lessons.title: Three of Those
lessons.concept: Building a Fraction from Copies of Its Unit Fraction

play.targetObjective: Make a fraction by shading that many copies of one part.
stepByStep: Look at how many parts the whole is cut into.
Each one of them is one of those parts.
Shade them one at a time, counting as you go.
Three quarters is three lots of one quarter. It is one number, not two.
play.kidTip: Every fraction is just so many copies of one piece.
play.audioPrompt: Shade that many of the parts, one at a time.

lessons.title: Writing It Down
lessons.concept: Reading a Picture as a Fraction

play.targetObjective: Write the fraction a picture shows.
stepByStep: Count the shaded parts.
Count all the parts.
The shaded ones go on top; all of them go underneath.
Read it out loud to check it sounds right.
play.kidTip: If you put them the other way up you have written something bigger than the whole.
play.audioPrompt: Count the shaded parts, then count all of them.

lessons.title: A Fraction of a Group
lessons.concept: Fractions of a Set Rather Than of One Object

play.targetObjective: Find a fraction of a set of objects.
stepByStep: The whole is the whole set, not one of the things in it.
Split the set into as many equal groups as the bottom number says.
Count how many are in one group.
Take as many groups as the top number says.
play.kidTip: A third of twelve marbles is four marbles — the whole is all twelve.
play.audioPrompt: Split the set into equal groups first.

lessons.title: One Jump Along
lessons.concept: Placing a Unit Fraction as a Number

play.targetObjective: Put a unit fraction in its place on a number line.
stepByStep: Look at how many equal jumps the line is cut into between 0 and 1.
Each jump is one of those parts.
Count one jump from zero.
Stop there. That is where the fraction lives.
play.kidTip: A fraction is not only part of a cake. It is a number with a place of its own.
play.audioPrompt: Count one jump from zero.

prompts.default: Put the marker on the fraction.

lessons.title: Count the Jumps
lessons.concept: Placing Any Proper Fraction as a Number

play.targetObjective: Put any fraction below one in its place on a number line.
stepByStep: Every jump along the line is one of the bottom number's parts.
The top number tells you how many jumps to take.
Count them from zero, one at a time.
Land on the mark, not between two.
play.kidTip: Top number, that many jumps. Bottom number, how big each jump is.
play.audioPrompt: Count that many jumps from zero.

prompts.default: Put the marker on the fraction.

lessons.title: What Is It Standing On?
lessons.concept: Reading a Fraction off a Number Line

play.targetObjective: Name the fraction a marker is sitting on.
stepByStep: Count the jumps from zero up to the marker. That is the top number.
Count all the jumps from 0 to 1. That is the bottom number.
Count jumps, never marks — there is always one more mark than jump.
Read it back and check it sounds smaller than one.
play.kidTip: The commonest slip here is counting the marks. Five marks means four jumps.
play.audioPrompt: Count the jumps from zero to the marker.

prompts.default: What number is the marker on?

lessons.title: Enough to Make One
lessons.concept: A Fraction with the Same Number Top and Bottom

play.targetObjective: Recognise that a fraction can be exactly one whole.
stepByStep: Count the jumps from 0 all the way to 1.
However many that is, that many of those parts make one whole.
So four quarters is one, and eight eighths is one.
Same number top and bottom always means one whole.
play.kidTip: A fraction does not have to be less than one. Some fractions are whole numbers.
play.audioPrompt: How many of those parts make one whole?

lessons.title: Past the One
lessons.concept: Improper Fractions as Numbers Beyond One

play.targetObjective: Place a fraction bigger than one on a number line.
stepByStep: This line carries on past 1.
The jumps are all the same size as before.
Count them from zero and go straight past the 1 without stopping.
A fraction bigger than one is still one number with one place.
play.kidTip: Seven quarters is just seven jumps of a quarter. Nothing stops at one.
play.audioPrompt: Keep counting past the one.

prompts.default: Put the marker on the fraction.

lessons.title: Cut Them All Again
lessons.concept: Equivalence Seen as Re-Cutting the Same Amount

play.targetObjective: Cut every part of a fraction into smaller ones and see the amount stay the same.
stepByStep: Look at how much is shaded before you start.
Cut every part into the same number of smaller pieces.
Watch the shading — it has not moved.
Count the new parts. There are more of them, and they are smaller.
play.kidTip: Cutting a pizza into more slices does not give you more pizza.
play.audioPrompt: Watch the shaded part while you cut. It does not move.

lessons.title: Two Names, One Amount
lessons.concept: Recognising Equivalent Fractions from Two Pictures

play.targetObjective: Recognise that two differently cut bars can show the same amount.
stepByStep: Look at how far the colour reaches on each bar. It is the same.
Now count the parts on each — they are cut differently.
So the same amount has two names.
Read both halves of a pair before you choose it.
play.kidTip: Equal fractions are not two amounts that are close. They are one amount with two names.
play.audioPrompt: Both bars have the same amount coloured in.

prompts.default: Which pair of names does this amount have?

lessons.title: Make It in Eighths
lessons.concept: Making an Equivalent Fraction with a Given Denominator

play.targetObjective: Write a fraction again with a larger denominator.
stepByStep: Work out how many smaller pieces each part has to become.
Cut every part into that many.
The shaded parts get cut as well, so there are that many times more of them.
Whatever you do to the bottom you do to the top — because you did it to both.
play.kidTip: You are not multiplying for the sake of it. You are cutting, and the shaded ones get cut too.
play.audioPrompt: How many smaller pieces does each part have to become?

prompts.default: Write it with the new bottom number.

lessons.title: Join Some Back Up
lessons.concept: Dividing Top and Bottom by a Shared Factor

play.targetObjective: Make a fraction simpler by joining parts back together.
stepByStep: Find a number that goes into the top and the bottom.
Join that many parts together, all along the bar.
The shading does not move, so the amount is the same.
Both numbers get smaller by the same factor.
play.kidTip: Joining up is cutting backwards. Nothing is lost either way.
play.audioPrompt: Both numbers divide by the same thing. Join them up.

lessons.title: As Simple As It Goes
lessons.concept: Reducing a Fraction by the Highest Common Factor

play.targetObjective: Reduce a fraction until nothing divides both numbers.
stepByStep: Join parts up while both numbers still share a factor.
Keep going. One step is often not enough.
Stop when the only number that goes into both is one.
If you can still halve both, you have not finished.
play.kidTip: Cancelling a two out of twelve twelfths is correct and unfinished. Keep going.
play.audioPrompt: Keep going while both numbers still divide by something.

prompts.default: Make it as simple as it goes.

lessons.title: Count the Pieces
lessons.concept: Comparing Fractions with the Same Denominator

play.targetObjective: Compare two fractions that are cut the same way.
stepByStep: Check the bottom numbers. They are the same.
That means every piece is the same size on both bars.
So you can simply count the coloured pieces.
More pieces of the same size is more.
play.kidTip: This is the easy one, and it is the reason the next one catches people out.
play.audioPrompt: Both bars are cut the same way. Count the pieces.

lessons.title: Bigger Bottom, Smaller Pieces
lessons.concept: Comparing Fractions with the Same Numerator

play.targetObjective: Compare two fractions with the same numerator by the size of their pieces.
stepByStep: Count the coloured pieces. There are the same number on each.
So the number of pieces is not what decides it.
Look at how big the pieces are.
Cutting a whole into more parts makes each part smaller. A bigger bottom number means smaller pieces.
play.kidTip: One eighth is smaller than one quarter, even though eight is bigger than four. Sharing between more people gives everybody less.
play.audioPrompt: The same number of pieces. So look at how big they are.

lessons.title: Only If It Is the Same Whole
lessons.concept: Comparison as Meaningless Across Different Wholes

play.targetObjective: Recognise that fractions of different wholes cannot be compared.
stepByStep: Look at the two wholes before you look at the colour.
They are not the same size to begin with.
So a half of one is not the same amount as a half of the other.
There is no answer to give. Saying so is the right answer.
play.kidTip: Half a mouse is not more than a quarter of an elephant, and it is not less either. The question is broken.
play.audioPrompt: Look at the two wholes before you look at the colour.

lessons.title: More or Less Than a Half
lessons.concept: Judging a Fraction Against a Benchmark

play.targetObjective: Judge whether a fraction is more or less than one half.
stepByStep: Work out half of the bottom number.
That many pieces would be exactly a half.
More pieces than that is more than a half.
Fewer is less. You never have to compare it with anything else.
play.kidTip: A half is the most useful number to measure other fractions against.
play.audioPrompt: Work out half of the bottom number first.

prompts.default: More or less than a half?

lessons.title: Make the Pieces Match
lessons.concept: Comparing Fractions by Finding a Common Denominator

play.targetObjective: Compare two fractions by re-cutting them to the same-sized pieces.
stepByStep: The pieces are different sizes, so counting them tells you nothing yet.
Find a number that both bottom numbers go into.
Cut both bars until every piece is that size.
Now the pieces match, so you can count them.
play.kidTip: You cannot compare four apples with three oranges until you turn them into the same fruit.
play.audioPrompt: Make the pieces the same size before you count them.

lessons.title: Loose Parts into Wholes
lessons.concept: Writing an Improper Fraction as a Mixed Number

play.targetObjective: Group loose parts into whole ones and write the amount as a mixed number.
stepByStep: Count how many parts it takes to make one whole.
Group that many together. That is one whole one.
Keep going while you still have enough for another.
Whatever is left over is the fraction part.
play.kidTip: Nothing is added or taken away. The same parts are just arranged differently.
play.audioPrompt: Group them into whole ones, and see what is left.

lessons.title: Wholes Back into Parts
lessons.concept: Writing a Mixed Number as an Improper Fraction

play.targetObjective: Break whole ones back into parts and write the amount as one fraction.
stepByStep: Every whole one breaks into the same number of parts as the bottom number.
Break them all up, one whole at a time.
Add the parts that were already loose.
Now the whole amount is written as one fraction.
play.kidTip: This is the last one run backwards. If you can do one, you can do the other.
play.audioPrompt: Break the whole ones up, then count every part.

lessons.title: Both Names, One Place
lessons.concept: Mixed Numbers and Improper Fractions on a Number Line

play.targetObjective: Place a mixed number on a number line and see its other name at the same point.
stepByStep: Find the whole number and go to that mark first.
Then count on in parts from there.
Stop on the mark, not between two.
Both names belong to that one mark, because they are the same number.
play.kidTip: Two names, one place. That is the whole idea.
play.audioPrompt: Find the whole number first, then count on in parts.

prompts.default: Put the marker on the number.

lessons.title: Add the Same Pieces
lessons.concept: Adding Fractions with the Same Denominator

play.targetObjective: Add two fractions that are already made of the same-sized pieces.
stepByStep: Look at the bottom numbers. They are the same, so the pieces are the same size.
That means you can just count them together.
Three eighths and two eighths is five eighths, the way three cats and two cats is five cats.
The bottom number does not change. You did not cut anything.
play.kidTip: Same-sized pieces can be counted. That is all adding is.
play.audioPrompt: The pieces are already the same size, so count them together.

lessons.title: Take Away the Same Pieces
lessons.concept: Subtracting Fractions with the Same Denominator

play.targetObjective: Take one fraction away from another when both are made of the same-sized pieces.
stepByStep: Check the bottom numbers first. Same number means same-sized pieces.
Count how many you have, then take away that many.
Count what is left on the strip.
The bottom number stays put, because the pieces never changed size.
play.kidTip: Taking away is counting backwards. The pieces still have to match.
play.audioPrompt: Both are the same size, so take one count from the other.

lessons.title: Why the Bottoms Do Not Add
lessons.concept: Why Denominators Are Not Added

play.targetObjective: Show on the strip that adding the bottom numbers gives an answer that is too small.
stepByStep: Somebody has added the tops and the bottoms. Put both fractions on the strip.
Half a strip and a third of a strip, laid end to end, reach past the halfway mark.
Two fifths does not even reach halfway. So it cannot be the total.
Cut both into the same-sized pieces first. Then, and only then, count.
play.kidTip: If your answer is smaller than what you started with, something has gone wrong.
play.audioPrompt: Somebody says this is the answer. Put both on the strip and see.

prompts.default: Show that this answer is too small.

lessons.title: When One Bottom Fits the Other
lessons.concept: Adding Fractions Where One Denominator Divides the Other

play.targetObjective: Add two fractions where only one of them needs re-cutting.
stepByStep: Look at the two bottom numbers. One of them goes into the other exactly.
That means only the bigger pieces need cutting up.
Cut them, so both strips are made of the same-sized pieces.
Now count them together, the way you did when they already matched.
play.kidTip: Cut the big pieces to match the small ones. Never the other way round.
play.audioPrompt: One of these already fits inside the other. Cut it and count.

prompts.default: Cut one to match, then count.

lessons.title: Make the Bottoms Match
lessons.concept: Adding Fractions with Unlike Denominators

play.targetObjective: Find a piece size both fractions can be cut into, then add them.
stepByStep: Neither bottom number goes into the other, so both strips need cutting.
Find a size they both fit into. Thirds and quarters both fit into twelfths.
Cut both, so every piece on the screen is the same size.
Now it is counting again.
play.kidTip: You are not changing the amounts. You are changing what the pieces are called.
play.audioPrompt: Find a size that fits both, cut them, then count.

lessons.title: Take Away Different Pieces
lessons.concept: Subtracting Fractions with Unlike Denominators

play.targetObjective: Cut both fractions to the same size, then take one away from the other.
stepByStep: Same first step as adding: the pieces have to match before anything happens.
Cut both strips into the size they both fit into.
Now take the second count away from the first.
Count what is left. The piece size has not changed.
play.kidTip: Matching first, always. Adding and taking away need exactly the same setup.
play.audioPrompt: Match the pieces first, then take one away from the other.

prompts.default: Match the pieces, then take away.

lessons.title: Add Whole Ones and Parts
lessons.concept: Adding Mixed Numbers

play.targetObjective: Add numbers that have whole ones and parts, and group any new whole one.
stepByStep: Add the whole ones first. They are easy and they get them out of the way.
Then the parts, which have to be cut to match like always.
If the parts add up to more than one whole, that whole joins the others.
Write what is left over as the fraction part.
play.kidTip: Wholes with wholes, parts with parts. Then see if the parts made another whole.
play.audioPrompt: Wholes first, then the parts. Watch for a new whole one.

prompts.default: Add the wholes, then the parts.

lessons.title: Break a Whole to Take Away
lessons.concept: Subtracting Mixed Numbers with Regrouping

play.targetObjective: Break one whole into parts so there are enough to take away.
stepByStep: Match the pieces first, as always.
Now look: there are not enough loose parts to take that many away.
Break one whole one up. It turns into that many more parts.
Now there are enough. Take them away, and count the whole ones left.
play.kidTip: This is the same exchange as borrowing in column subtraction, done with parts.
play.audioPrompt: There are not enough parts. Break a whole one up first.

prompts.default: Break a whole, then take away.

lessons.title: A Fraction of an Amount
lessons.concept: Finding a Fraction of a Whole Number

play.targetObjective: Find a fraction of an amount by sharing it into equal groups and taking some of them.
stepByStep: The bottom number tells you how many equal groups to make.
Share the whole amount out into that many groups.
The top number tells you how many of those groups to take.
Count what is in the groups you took. That is the answer.
play.kidTip: Divide by the bottom, multiply by the top. In that order, and the numbers stay small.
play.audioPrompt: Share it into equal groups first, then take the ones you need.

lessons.title: Copies of a Fraction
lessons.concept: Multiplying a Fraction by a Whole Number

play.targetObjective: Multiply a fraction by a whole number by making that many copies of it.
stepByStep: Four times two fifths means four copies of two fifths, laid end to end.
Count all the shaded pieces. There are eight of them.
They are still fifths — making copies did not change the size of a piece.
Eight fifths is more than one whole, so it can also be written as one and three fifths.
play.kidTip: Only the count goes up. The pieces stay the size they were.
play.audioPrompt: Make that many copies, then count the pieces.

lessons.title: A Fraction of a Fraction
lessons.concept: Multiplying Two Fractions with an Area Model

play.targetObjective: Multiply two fractions by shading one across a grid and the other down it.
stepByStep: Shade the first fraction across the grid, in columns.
Now shade the second one down the grid, in rows.
Some squares are shaded twice. Those are the ones in both fractions.
Count them, out of all the squares. That is a fraction of a fraction.
play.kidTip: Two thirds of three quarters is smaller than either one. Taking a part of a part always is.
play.audioPrompt: Shade one across and one down. The answer is where they cross.

lessons.title: Cancel Before You Multiply
lessons.concept: Simplifying Before Multiplying Fractions

play.targetObjective: Divide out a shared factor across the diagonal before multiplying, so the numbers stay small.
stepByStep: You could multiply straight across, but the numbers get big and then need cutting down again.
Look diagonally: a top number and a bottom number often share a factor.
Divide both of them by it. The answer does not change, because you divided a top and a bottom.
Now multiply the small numbers that are left.
play.kidTip: Cancelling early is the same work done in an easier order.
play.audioPrompt: Look for a factor across the diagonal before you multiply.

lessons.title: Smaller, Not Bigger
lessons.concept: Multiplication as Scaling

play.targetObjective: Say whether multiplying will make an amount bigger, smaller or leave it alone, before working it out.
stepByStep: Do not work it out. Just look at the fraction doing the multiplying.
Less than one whole? Then you are taking a part of the amount, so the answer is smaller.
More than one whole? Then there is more than all of it, so the answer is bigger.
Exactly one whole leaves the amount exactly as it was.
play.kidTip: Multiplying only makes things bigger when you multiply by more than one. Nobody tells you that for years.
play.audioPrompt: Look at the fraction first. Is it less than one whole, or more?
